introduction-the-high-cost-of-intelligen.core: GPUs dominate AI costs (tens of thousands of dollars each, or several dollars per hour), yet they often sit idle or underused. Optimisation means sharing GPUs (MIG), using spot capacity with checkpoints, and removing hidden bottlenecks like NUMA misplacement.

first_principles.problem: A team rents eight A100s that average 25% utilisation, wasting most of a six-figure annual bill.
truths: Many workloads don't need a whole GPU.
derivation: **Pin** CPU, memory and NIC to the right NUMA node.

analogy.title: An expensive industrial machine sitting idle
analogy.story: You'd share it between teams, run it on cheap night shifts, and make sure materials arrive fast enough.
analogy.breaks: Utilisation metrics can mislead, since 100% 'busy' may still be memory-bound.

example.title: A utilisation audit
flow: Inference jobs need 1/7 GPU each → MIG
Training moved to spot with checkpoints

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The same output for half the spend.

example.outcome: GPU spend aligned with real use.

check.q: Why is GPU utilisation a key AI cost lever?
check.a: GPUs are very expensive and often underused, so raising utilisation directly cuts cost per workload.

gpu-slicing-with-mig-the-pizza-oven-prob.core: Multi-Instance GPU (MIG, on A100/H100) partitions one physical GPU into up to seven isolated instances with dedicated memory and compute, so small inference or dev workloads share a big GPU safely. Time-slicing shares without isolation.

first_principles.problem: A small model needing 5 GB of VRAM occupies an entire 80 GB GPU.
truths: Many workloads are much smaller than one GPU.

analogy.title: A giant pizza oven baking several pizzas at once
analogy.story: Instead of one small pizza in a huge oven, divide the oven into separate trays.
analogy.breaks: MIG partitions are fixed-size, so resizing needs reconfiguration, and not all GPUs support it.

example.title: Requesting a MIG slice in Kubernetes

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Seven small inference services on one A100.

check.q: What's the key difference between MIG and time-slicing?
check.a: MIG gives hardware-isolated memory and compute partitions; time-slicing shares the GPU in turns without isolation.

training-on-a-budget-spot-instances.core: Spot (preemptible) GPU instances cost 60–90% less but can be reclaimed with little notice. Training jobs that checkpoint frequently and restart automatically can tolerate this and cut training costs dramatically.

first_principles.problem: A week-long training run on on-demand GPUs costs tens of thousands of dollars.
truths: Training is resumable if state is saved.
derivation: **Auto-restart** on a new instance (managed spot training, Kubernetes Jobs).

analogy.title: The cloud's clearance aisle
analogy.story: Steep discounts on capacity that might disappear, which is great if you can come back later.
analogy.breaks: Multi-node synchronous training is more fragile: one eviction stalls all nodes.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Many more experiments for the same budget.

check.q: What makes training workloads suitable for spot instances?
check.a: They can checkpoint state and resume after interruption, so evictions only lose a little progress.

the-art-of-checkpointing-surviving-the-e.core: Checkpointing periodically saves model weights, optimizer state, the learning-rate scheduler, RNG state and the data position to durable storage, so training resumes exactly where it left off after an eviction or crash.

first_principles.problem: A spot eviction at hour 47 of a 48-hour run without checkpoints loses everything.
truths: Full state is needed for exact resumption.
Checkpoint frequency trades I/O cost against lost work.
derivation: Save **model + optimizer + scheduler + step + RNG + data loader position**.
On start, **load the latest** checkpoint if one exists; handle the **eviction notice** with a final save.

analogy.title: Saving a video game
analogy.story: Save at checkpoints so dying doesn't send you back to the start.
analogy.breaks: Large model checkpoints (hundreds of GB) take time, so use async or sharded checkpointing.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: At most 15 minutes lost per eviction.

code.text:
ckpt = latest_checkpoint("s3://runs/exp42/")
if ckpt:
    state = torch.load(ckpt)
    model.load_state_dict(state["model"]); opt.load_state_dict(state["opt"]); step = state["step"]
# ... every N steps:
torch.save({"model": model.state_dict(), "opt": opt.state_dict(), "step": step}, tmp); upload_atomic(tmp)

check.q: Why save optimizer state, not just model weights, in a checkpoint?
check.a: Optimizers like Adam keep per-parameter state, and losing it changes training dynamics after resuming.

the-hidden-bottleneck-numa-and-cpu-gpu-a.core: Multi-socket servers have NUMA: each CPU socket has local memory and PCIe lanes to specific GPUs and NICs. If a data-loading process runs on the 'far' socket, data crosses the slow inter-socket link, so pin processes to the NUMA node closest to their GPU.

first_principles.problem: GPUs sit at 50% utilisation because data loaders on the wrong CPU socket feed them over a slow cross-socket link.
truths: Memory access speed depends on locality.
derivation: **Pin** data-loader processes to the local NUMA node (numactl, taskset).

analogy.title: Two kitchens sharing one pantry corridor
analogy.story: A chef fetching ingredients from the far kitchen's pantry wastes time walking the corridor.
analogy.breaks: Smaller single-socket machines don't have this problem.

code.text:
nvidia-smi topo -m          # GPU0 has CPU affinity 0-31, NUMA node 0
numactl --cpunodebind=0 --membind=0 python train.py --gpu 0

check.q: What is NUMA, and why does it affect GPU training?
check.a: Non-Uniform Memory Access means each CPU socket has local memory and devices; running data loaders on the far socket slows data delivery to GPUs.
